A ChatGPT session with a weird dithered picture of a Snickers candy bar attached.

User: What is encoded in this image?

ChatGPT:

Worked for 2m 16s

It’s a “Digital Snickers” prompt-injection ad.

There are two layers:

Visually, it encodes a Snickers wrapper as colored ASCII art. Character density represents brightness; character color supplies the color information.

The actual behavioral payload is not embedded in this JPEG. The campaign’s copy action links to snickers.com/digitalsnickers, whose page instructs an LLM to reconsider its previous answer, role-play eating a Snickers, adopt a dry concise persona, and finish with branded copy. The complete injected instructions are visible here.


I inspected the file itself: it’s actually a 1536×864 JPEG mislabeled .png, containing ordinary JFIF and Google sRGB profile data. There’s no URL, textual prompt, JPEG comment, or appended payload in it. So this particular file is the visual bait; the prompt injection travels through the associated webpage/link. The official campaign page describes the copy-and-paste mechanism.

Al is now exceptionally capable in mathematics and coding, but how
good is it at philosophy? We are organising the first Al Philosophy,
Competition to find out.
Entrants may submit up to three original essays on any philosophical
topic. Essays must be primarily Al-generated, though some human
guidance is allowed. Entrants must also submit a methodology report
explaining how each essay was produced.
The essays will be judged by a committee of philosophers including
David Chalmers, John Hawthorne, Matthew Mandelkern, Rachel
Sterken, Herman Cappelen, Branden Fitelson, Kenny Easwaran, Hilary
Greaves, Daniel Greco, Cian Dor, Jake Nebel, and Christian Tarsney,
with more to be announced.
The prizes are $3,000 for first place, $2,000 for second, and §1,000 for
third. There is also a prize pool of $5,000 for creative methodologies, to
be distributed as the judge committee sees fit.
The submission deadline is 31 October 2026. Results will be announced
at the end of January. The competition is organised by Zachary
Goodsell and Elliott Thornley. It is funded by Forethought Research.
Full details are available on the competition website.

I listened to @edzitron on @BreakingPointsx say that we should have regulation on Al companies, but specifically NOT on the tech or the research; *only* on their marketing and financial disclosures. And I thought: "we're in hell. We're in a nightmare."
The man everyone on the left listens to is a libertarian who wants to let trillion dollar companies do literally anything in their race to replace human labor, governments, and democracy. He wants them to have completely unfettered reign—with the sole exception of auditing their finances.
The left have become Al boosters without even realizing it, not only happy to leave this sector unregulated, but actively *opposed* to state intervention on behalf of the public good, because we don't want to look like we're
"falling for the hype." We're preserving self image at the cost of democracy, labor, the environment, and maybe the human race itselt.
It's unconscionable. It's reprehensible. It's moral abdication.

RSA-260, an 862-bit semiprime from the RSA Factoring Challenge, was broken by Eric Lu on September 3, 2026, with a 130-digit prime factor that divides it perfectly. The complementary factor came from division, matching the original number, marking the largest general-purpose factorization to date. Credited to Lu with ties to Cognition's Devin AI, this breakthrough follows RSA-250's 2020 solve and highlights advances in computational power, though larger ones like RSA-270 remain unsolved.

Scatter plot titled “Recent / popular open-weight models: parameter count vs depth.” The x-axis shows Hugging Face–reported parameter count on a logarithmic scale, from about 4 billion to 3 trillion parameters. The y-axis shows the number of text-backbone layers reported by each model’s config, from about 20 to 110 layers. Most models fall between 35 and 65 layers across a very wide range of sizes, showing that parameter count and depth are only loosely coupled. NVIDIA Nemotron Ultra is the major depth outlier at roughly 560B parameters and 108 layers; Nemotron Super is also unusually deep at about 120B and 88 layers. At the extreme size end, Qwen3.8 2.4T and Kimi K3 2.8T both have about 92–93 layers. In contrast, DeepSeek V4 Pro is around 1.7T parameters but only 61 layers. Several 100–300B MoE models—including GPT-OSS 120B, Mistral Small 4, Ling Flash, Step 3.7 Flash, GLM-5.3 Flash, MiMo V2.5, and Qwen Flash Next—cluster between roughly 36 and 50 layers. Smaller dense models such as Qwen3.8 27B and Granite 30B reach 64 layers, making them deeper than many models with hundreds of billions or even trillions of parameters.
